learn.title: Why proofs
learn.body: In geometry we do not just notice that something is true. We show why it must be true, using facts we already accept. That chain of reasons is called a proof.

learn.title: If-then statements
learn.body: A conditional has the form: if $p$, then $q$. The $p$ part is the hypothesis and the $q$ part is the conclusion. The converse swaps them: if $q$, then $p$. A statement can be true while its converse is false.

learn.title: Counterexamples
learn.body: To show a statement is false, one counterexample is enough. The statement all prime numbers are odd fails for 2, which is prime and even. But examples alone never prove a statement true. A proof must cover every case.

learn.title: Prove vertical angles are equal
learn.body: Two lines cross. Call the angles around the crossing 1, 2, 3, 4 in order, so 1 and 3 are opposite.
steps: Angles 1 and 2 are a linear pair, so $\angle1+\angle2=180^\circ$.
Angles 2 and 3 are a linear pair, so $\angle2+\angle3=180^\circ$.

learn.body: In a proof, every statement needs a reason: a given fact, a definition, or a rule you already proved.

questions.prompt: In the statement if it rains, the ground is wet, which part is the hypothesis?
questions.explanation: The hypothesis is the part after if. The part after then is the conclusion.

questions.prompt: What is the converse of if a shape is a square, then it is a rectangle?
choices: If a shape is not a square, then it is not a rectangle
If a shape is a rectangle, then it has four sides
If a shape is a rectangle, then it is a square
questions.explanation: The converse swaps hypothesis and conclusion.

questions.prompt: Is the converse of that statement true?
choices: No, many rectangles are not squares
questions.explanation: A rectangle with sides 2 and 5 is a counterexample. A statement can be true while its converse is false.

questions.prompt: Which number is a counterexample to every odd number is prime?
questions.explanation: 9 is odd but equals $3\cdot3$, so it is not prime. The others are prime.

questions.prompt: One \_\_ is enough to show a statement is false.
questions.explanation: A single case that breaks the statement disproves it. A single case that fits does not prove anything.

questions.prompt: Put the proof that vertical angles are equal in order.
steps: Angles 1 and 2 are a linear pair: $\angle1+\angle2=180^\circ$
Angles 2 and 3 are a linear pair: $\angle2+\angle3=180^\circ$
questions.explanation: Two linear-pair facts give two equal sums, and subtracting the shared angle finishes the proof.

questions.prompt: Match the term to its meaning.
pairs: A case that breaks a statement
questions.explanation: These four words are the vocabulary of logical statements in geometry.
